steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI/HRI paper exploring whether large language models can support variable autonomy and shared control in human-robot teaming. Cover the background on shared control and language, why LLMs are promising, our VR multi-agent prototype and user study, the contributions, and a note on the exploratory nature of the work.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- From machines as tools to machines as partners; shared control and variable autonomy need communication
- Language, Joint Actions, and the rise of LLMs
- Why LLMs fit shared control and variable autonomy (and the challenges)
- Our system and user study
- Contributions
- Scope: simulated agents and exploratory approach

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Tools to partners
- past 10 to 15 years: shift from machines as useful tools to partners in human-like collaboration
- true peer-to-peer human-machine interaction still far off
- balance user's need for autonomy vs robot's capabilities and level of autonomy
- variable autonomy and shared control as research areas
- shared control: optimal sharing of control between human and machine for effective, efficient system
- needs communication to negotiate and adapt sharing of control
- spoken language, vehicle of thought, essential for human-human collaboration
- NLP important in robotics and AI since infancy: Winograd's SHRDLU, Nilsson et al.'s Shakey the Robot

## Joint Actions and LLMs
- Joint Actions: popular approach to human-human cooperation
- could be extrapolated to human-machine cooperation
- joint activity and communication inseparable; needs common language -> machine's natural language ability
- recent NLP breakthroughs; Transformer architecture -> LLMs such as GPT and BERT
- competences: translation, question-answering, creative writing, medical diagnostics

## LLMs for shared control / variable autonomy
- interpret natural language, respond dynamically
- intuitive interaction, uses our propensity for verbal communication
- human-like responses -> mediate between humans and autonomous agents; common medium to negotiate and adjust
- linguistic bridge: intentions, feedback, commands
- challenge: LLM strengths don't require mapping commands to specific output bound by physical capabilities
- existing work: GPT might already allow natural-language coordination with a robot
- aim: explore area from feasibility and user perspective

## System and study
- LLM-powered multi-agent system in VR-based simulation framework
- user fulfils simple tasks by talking to three simulated robot agents, each with own GPT core
- user study, 12 participants: engagement, naturalness, suitability of GPT
- key interest: user reactions when agents did not behave as anticipated

## Contributions
- Unity-based framework, voice-controlled multi-agent system in VR, single user + scalable number of LLM-based agents
- understanding of user strategies and behaviors in LLM-based simulated multi-robot environment
- lessons learned on feasibility/practicability; naturalness, adaptability of GPT and users; framework improvements

## Scope
- simulated agents on purpose: focus on communication interface, not mechanics of physical robots
- relevant to hypothetical real-world applications and theoretical explorations of LLMs in robotics
- exploratory methods well-established; also in HRI (review of qualitative research approaches)
- framework as exploratory tool for researchers outside AI or traditional robotics

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the past 10 to 15 years there has been a significant shift from machines being just useful tools towards machines as partners in more complex collaboration tasks that are human like. Still, true peer-to-peer interaction between humans and machines like robots has a long way to go before it resembles interaction and collaboration between humans. For humans to cooperate seamlessly with autonomous tools such as robots, a delicate balance has to be found between the user's need for autonomy and the capabilities and level of autonomous behavior of the robot. Here concepts like variable autonomy and shared control have been important research areas. Shared control especially tries to find optimal configurations for how control is shared between a human and an autonomous machine like a robot, so that the whole system is as effective and efficient as possible. At its core it needs an effective way for the parties to communicate so they can negotiate and adapt how control is shared. This communication between humans and machines can use many input and output modalities, but spoken language, as a vehicle of thought, has played an essential role in communication and collaboration between humans. Natural language has a long history of exploration in fields like human-machine cooperation and AI. NLP has been a very significant branch of robotics and AI research since the beginning, with foundational works like Winograd's SHRDLU and Nilsson et al.'s Shakey the Robot.

For language to be an effective means for collaboration though, research has suggested the overarching concept of Joint Actions, which has become a popular approach to understanding cooperation between humans. This concept could be extrapolated to cooperation between humans and machines, as prior work has suggested. Since this perspective says that joint activity and communication cannot be separated and that communication needs a common language, progress in this field depends heavily on the machine's ability to understand and communicate in natural language. And the field of NLP has had significant breakthroughs recently. These advancements, most notably the development of the Transformer architecture, have led to LLMs such as GPT and BERT. They have shown competences in translation, question-answering, creative writing and even medical diagnostics.

We think the ability of LLMs to interpret natural language input and respond to it dynamically shows their potential use for shared control and variable autonomy. By design these systems can interact in a way that is intuitive to humans, using our natural tendency for verbal communication as seen when humans cooperate with each other. LLMs can generate responses that convincingly resemble human dialogue, so they are well-suited to mediate communication between humans and autonomous agents, and to give a common medium in which shared control and variable autonomy can be negotiated and adjusted dynamically. The linguistic bridge of LLMs could let humans and machines articulate intentions, feedback, and commands to each other, which would help implement shared control and variable autonomy in a way that is intuitive and fits human cognitive processes. Of course there are also some inherent challenges. The use cases where LLMs excel do not need spoken commands to be mapped to a very specific output that is bound by what an autonomous agent can physically do. Still, existing work has shown that available LLMs such as GPT might already allow communication and coordination with a robot based on natural language. In this paper we want to explore this up and coming research area from a feasibility perspective and also from a user perspective.

- our system: LLM-powered multi-agent system in VR-based simulation; three simulated robot agents, each with own GPT core; user study with 12 participants; reactions when agents misbehave
- contributions: Unity-based voice-controlled framework; user strategies and behaviors; lessons learned and possible improvements
- simulated agents on purpose: communication interface, not robot mechanics
- exploratory approach well-established, also in HRI (review of qualitative approaches); framework as tool for researchers outside AI or traditional robotics

The use cases where LLMs excel do not need spoken commands to be mapped to a very specific output that is bound by what an autonomous agent can physically do. Still, existing work has shown that available LLMs such as GPT might already allow communication and coordination with a robot based on natural language. In this paper we want to explore this up and coming research area from a feasibility perspective and also from a user perspective.

For this we designed a multi-agent system powered by an LLM as part of a VR-based simulation framework. In the virtual game world, the user can do simple tasks just by talking to three simulated robot agents, and each agent is controlled by its own GPT core. With the prototype we ran a user study with 12 participants to look at how humans engaged with the simulated robot agents, how natural it felt to them and how well GPT suited this use case. One key interest was understanding how users reacted and acted, especially when the GPT-based simulated robot agents did not behave as expected, which shows the nuances of human-agent interaction. So the contribution of this paper is

- The design and architecture of a framework based on Unity for a voice-controlled multi-agent system in VR, which can be used to explore the interaction and control dynamics between one user and a scalable number of simulated robot agents based on LLMs.

- From our study, a better understanding of the strategies and behaviors of users when they are confronted with a simulated multi-robot environment based on LLMs.

- Lessons learned about the feasibility and practicability of adapting GPT-based LLMs to interact with simulated multi-robot agents. This includes reflections on how natural these interactions are and how GPT and its users adapt in unforeseen scenarios, and also possible improvements to the framework that could inspire other similar systems.

In addition to these contributions, it is important to say that our Unity simulation framework uses simulated robot agents. We deliberately focus on the communication interface between humans and LLM-powered agents and not on the mechanical intricacies of physical robots and actions. This lets us examine human-agent communication in detail, which is relevant both to hypothetical real-world applications and to theoretical explorations of what LLMs can do in robotics.

Our approach is exploratory, but exploratory research methods are well-established in the literature as a way to investigate areas where there is limited pre-existing knowledge or to give a comprehensive understanding of a new or complex issue. This also applies in the field of HRI, as a review of similar qualitative research approaches shows. In the same way our simulation framework is an exploratory tool, aimed specifically at other researchers outside of AI or traditional robotics who may want to investigate further the interaction dynamics between human users and simulated LLM-based robot agents.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Over the past 10 to 15 years, we have seen a significant shift from machines being merely useful tools towards machines as partners in more complex, human-like collaboration tasks [1]. Still, true peer-to-peer interaction between humans and machines such as robots has a long way to go before it resembles inter-human interaction and collaboration. For humans to cooperate seamlessly with autonomous tools such as robots, a delicate balance must be struck between a user's need for autonomy [2] and the robot's capabilities and level of autonomous behavior. In this context, concepts such as variable autonomy and shared control have been vital research areas. Shared control in particular aims to find optimal configurations of how control can be shared between a human and an autonomous machine such as a robot, so that the overall system is as effective and efficient as possible [3]. At its core, it requires an effective way for the parties to communicate in order to negotiate and adapt the sharing of control [4,5,6]. While such communication between humans and machines can rely on a variety of input and output modalities, spoken language, as a vehicle of thought, has played an essential role in human-human communication and collaboration [7]. The exploration of natural language in fields like human-machine cooperation and AI has a long history. NLP has been a highly significant branch of robotics and AI research since its infancy, spearheaded by foundational works like Winograd's SHRDLU [8] and Nilsson et al.'s Shakey the Robot [9].

Conceptually, however, for language to be an effective means for collaboration, research has suggested the overarching concept of Joint Actions [7], which has become a popular approach to understanding human-human cooperation [10,11,12]. This concept could potentially be extrapolated to cooperation between humans and machines, as suggested by [4]. Since this perspective holds that joint activity and communication are inseparable and that communication requires a common language, progress in this field is heavily tied to the machine's ability to understand and communicate in natural language. It is in this context that the field of NLP has recently seen significant breakthroughs. These advancements, epitomized by the development of the Transformer architecture by [13], have led to the emergence of LLMs such as GPT and BERT [14] [15]. These have demonstrated competences in fields such as translation [16], question-answering [17], creative writing [18] and even medical diagnostics [19,20].

We believe that the capability of LLMs to interpret natural language inputs and respond to them dynamically highlights their potential utility for shared control and variable autonomy. By design, these systems can engage in a form of interaction that is intuitive to humans, leveraging our natural propensity for verbal communication as seen in cooperative human-to-human interactions. Their ability to generate responses that convincingly resemble human dialogue makes LLMs well-suited for mediating communication between humans and autonomous agents, providing a common medium through which shared control and variable autonomy can be negotiated and dynamically adjusted. The linguistic bridge that LLMs provide could allow humans and machines to articulate intentions, feedback, and commands, thereby facilitating shared control and variable autonomy in a way that is intuitive and aligned with human cognitive processes. Of course, there are inherent challenges as well. The use cases in which LLMs excel do not require mapping spoken commands to a very specific output bound by the physical capabilities of an autonomous agent. Still, existing work has shown that available LLMs such as GPT might already allow communication and coordination with a robot based on natural language [21]. This paper aims to explore this up and coming research area from both a feasibility and a user perspective.

To this end, we have designed an LLM-powered multi-agent system as part of a VR-based simulation framework. In the virtual game world, a user can fulfill simple tasks solely by conversing with three simulated robot agents, each controlled by its own GPT core. Using the prototype, we conducted a user study with 12 participants to investigate how humans engaged with the simulated robot agents, how natural it felt to them and how well GPT was suited for this use case. A key area of interest was understanding user reactions and actions, especially when the GPT-based simulated robot agents did not behave as anticipated, highlighting the nuances of human-agent interaction. Consequently, the contribution of this paper consists of

- The design and architecture of a Unity-based framework for a voice-controlled multi-agent system in VR, with which the interaction and control dynamics between a single user and a scalable number of LLM-based simulated robot agents can be explored.

- Based on our study, an improved understanding of users' strategies and behaviors when confronted with an LLM-based simulated multi-robot environment.

- A set of lessons learned on the feasibility and practicability of adapting GPT-based LLMs to interact with simulated multi-robot agents, including reflections on the naturalness of such interactions and the adaptability of GPT and its users in unforeseen scenarios, as well as possible improvements to the framework that could inspire other similar systems.

In addition to these contributions, it is important to note that our Unity simulation framework uses simulated robot agents, deliberately focusing on the communication interface between humans and LLM-powered agents rather than on the mechanical intricacies of physical robots and actions. This enables a detailed examination of human-agent communication, relevant both to hypothetical real-world applications and to theoretical explorations of LLM capabilities in robotics.

While our approach is exploratory, exploratory research methods are well-established in the literature as a means to investigate areas with limited pre-existing knowledge or to provide a comprehensive understanding of a new or complex issue. This also applies to the field of HRI, as demonstrated by the review from [22] of similar qualitative research approaches. In the same vein, our simulation framework is an exploratory tool, aimed specifically at researchers outside the field of AI or traditional robotics who may want to further investigate the interaction dynamics between human users and simulated LLM-based robot agents.
